a OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 70
i OurBigBook.com
Make heterogeneous electron transfer fast relative to delivery of reactant, usually by applying sufficient overpotential so that its surface concentration approaches zero. Use excess supporting electrolyte to suppress migration. For purely diffusional transient transport, suppress uncontrolled convection; for a rotating disk electrode, controlled convection supplies the bulk while diffusion across the thin interfacial boundary layer limits the current. A limiting current that no longer increases with driving potential is the characteristic test; a large current alone is not sufficient.

Words: 66 Articles: 1
a OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 66
ii OurBigBook.com
The midpoint potential Em​ characterizes the redox couple under specified solution conditions: it is the potential at which oxidized and reduced forms have equal activities, or equal concentrations in the corresponding formal-potential convention. For a reversible cyclic voltammogram it is estimated by (Epa​+Epc​)/2. It approximates the formal redox potential when the usual reversibility and diffusion assumptions apply; it is not the potential halfway along a scan chosen arbitrarily.

b

Words: 171 Articles: 1
51 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 171
b OurBigBook.com
All three marked points are at strongly oxidizing potentials, where X is depleted at the electrode: cX​(0)≃0. Assuming only X initially in bulk, cX+​(∞)=0 and cX​(∞)=cb​. Oxidation produces X+ at the interface.
  • A: the largest steady limiting current corresponds to the fastest rotation and thinnest diffusion boundary layer. X rises steeply from zero to cb​; X+ falls steeply from its surface value to zero.
  • B: slower rotation gives a thicker layer and shallower gradients, hence a smaller limiting current.
  • C: the nonrotating electrode gives the peaked, subsequently decaying current. Its diffusion layer continues to broaden with time, approximately as Dt​, giving the broadest and shallowest profiles at the indicated late-scan point.
For equal diffusion coefficients, the two concentration profiles are complementary, cX​+cX+​=cb​. More generally equality of their interfacial molar fluxes requires DX​cX′​(0)=−DX+​cX+′​(0), so the product surface concentration need not equal cb​. A and B are approximately steady hydrodynamic profiles; C is a time-dependent diffusion profile.

i OurBigBook.com
Read the potential labels rather than the alphabetical order: b, the less negative event, is Q+e−⇌Q∙−; a, the more negative event, is Q∙−+e−⇌Q2−. These are the first and second reductions respectively, with the reverse branches giving the corresponding oxidations. The second electron is harder to add to an already negatively charged species.

ii

Words: 104 Articles: 1
c OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 104
ii OurBigBook.com
Event a probes electron transfer between the semiquinone and dianion. Benzoquinone's smaller framework localizes charge and undergoes a greater change in bonding and solvation on this reduction; a larger effective reorganization barrier can make its heterogeneous transfer insufficiently fast for Nernst equilibrium on the 50mVs−1 time scale. Anthraquinone's extended framework distributes the added charge and can support the more reversible response seen here.
This is a kinetic interpretation of quasi-reversibility, not a claim that benzoquinone cannot be reduced. Follow-up chemistry or adsorption can also distort peak separation and return-current ratios; scan-rate-dependent measurements would distinguish them from slow electron transfer. A single trace does not uniquely identify the cause.

iii

Words: 119 Articles: 1
c OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 119
iii OurBigBook.com
A useful electrode-surface scheme for the proposed ECEC mechanism is
AQ+e−​AQ∙−+CO2​​AQCO2∙−​+e−​AQCO22−​+CO2​​AQ(CO2​)22−​.
(1)
Electron-transfer arrows occur at the electrode, whereas both capture steps occur in the adjacent solution layer. CO2​ is attacked by an oxygen-centered nucleophilic component of the reduced quinone, forming an O-carbonate linkage rather than simply physically adsorbing on neutral AQ.
At potentials more negative than −2.0V, direct second reduction of any unbound semiquinone is also accessible: AQ∙−→AQ2−, followed by carbonate formation. Thus the fully reduced unbound and mono-adduct species can feed the bis-adduct, and the drawing should include CO2​ transport into the layer and adduct transport away. ECEC is the proposed sequence; competing EECC transfer/capture ordering is possible at such negative potentials.

iv

Words: 179 Articles: 1
c OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 179
iv OurBigBook.com
Peak I is the cathodic reduction shifted positive of the unbound AQ∙−/AQ2− event, consistent with reduction of the CO2​-bound semiquinone to mono-carbonate dianion. Peak II is the corresponding relatively negative-potential return oxidation of mono-carbonate dianion. Peak III, appearing farther positive on the faster return scan, is consistent with direct oxidation of the more strongly protected bis-carbonate dianion, followed by CO2​ release.
This assignment is consistent with binding making the reduced species harder to oxidize. At slow scan, chemical interconversion and CO2​ dissociation can feed the easier mono-carbonate oxidation pathway; at fast scan a larger fraction of kinetically retained bis-adduct survives to its direct oxidation potential. The two separated reductions also show that initial capture and its associated potential shift are not sufficient to make every ECEC step a single equilibrated two-electron wave.
These traces support coupled electron-transfer/binding chemistry but do not determine every microscopic rate constant or exclude EECC pathways. The peak assignments are species-family assignments within the stated mechanism, rather than proof of a unique elementary sequence from voltammetry alone.

v

Words: 124 Articles: 1
c OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 124
v OurBigBook.com
Within the stated ECEC model and with CO2​ genuinely in large excess, its concentration is effectively constant. Both capture steps are then pseudo-first-order in the quinone species, and at the same scan rate the faradaic current is linear in bulk AQ concentration.
The sketch therefore retains the peak potentials, sweep directions and relative features of the 200mVs−1 trace, including the positive-potential return feature III, but reduces the faradaic current scale by a factor of ten. Charging/background current need not scale with AQ concentration and should be shown separately. A changed normalized shape would indicate effects outside this simple scaling limit, such as CO2​ depletion, adsorption or reactions between quinone species.

vi OurBigBook.com
The target dianion consumes two electrons per molecule, so
ηF​=ne−​2nproduct​​=18.22(7.8)​=0.857,
(2)
giving 85.7% Faradaic yield. Of the passed electron equivalents, 2.6mmol are not accounted for by the quantified bis-adduct.
They can reside in incompletely captured reduced quinones, other reduction products or parasitic solvent/proton/CO2​ chemistry. The data do not identify one unique loss pathway. The starting solution contains 50mmol BQ, so the target product represents only 15.6% of that inventory; low bulk conversion alone does not explain a sub-unity Faradaic yield, because unreacted BQ has consumed no charge.

Words: 124
a OurBigBook.com
Write Me=CH3​. The alternating-vertex cubane A is Li4​Me4​; replacing one or two methyl vertices gives B=Li4​Me3​X and C=Li4​Me2​X2​. Balanced redistributions are
A+LiX⇌B+MeLi,A+2LiX⇌C+2MeLi.
(3)
The smaller aggregate has composition D=Li2​MeX, since the conventional masses 2(7)+15+80=109 or 2(7)+15+127=156 match the supplied values. Thus A+4LiX⇌4D is another balanced redistribution.
For the structures, place Li on one tetrahedral set of cube corners and Me/X on the complementary set, joining adjacent unlike vertices. A contains four Me vertices, B three Me and one X, and C two of each. D is a four-membered alternating Li-Me-Li-X ring. The quoted relative masses use conventional elemental masses; a fully 6Li-enriched D would be approximately two mass units lighter, without changing its composition.

b

Words: 154 Articles: 1
52 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 154
b OurBigBook.com
Useful isotope-selection factors include spin and quadrupole moment, gyromagnetic ratio, natural abundance or enrichment, sensitivity at the available field, line widths and relaxation, chemical-shift dispersion and the couplings needed for structural assignment. Both lithium isotopes are quadrupolar, but 6Li has a much smaller quadrupole moment and often much narrower lines, allowing inequivalent sites and carbon-lithium couplings to be resolved. Enrichment compensates its low natural abundance and removes isotope-mixture complexity.
Fully enriched 7Li would generally be more sensitive but broader in these aggregates. Its chemical-shift pattern would remain chemically similar, although isotope shifts and dynamics can make small differences. Resolved H-Li couplings increase in frequency approximately with γ7​/γ6​=2.67 and have different multiplicities because I changes from 1 to 3/2: n equivalent Li nuclei give 2nI+1 lines. If such long-range proton couplings remain unresolved, the main visible difference can instead be broadened lines. One should not invent resolved multiplets absent from the printed spectra.

c

Words: 106 Articles: 1
52 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 106
c OurBigBook.com
The nucleus-count ratios H:6Li are A, 12:4=3:1; B, 9:4; C, 6:4=3:2; D, 3:2. Enrichment changes which isotope is counted but not these stoichiometric ratios.
Quantitative lithium integration requires adequate excitation bandwidth, a suitable calibrated pulse, acquisition of the entire broad as well as narrow signal, correct baseline/phasing and no differential saturation. Recycle delays should be long relative to the slowest relevant longitudinal relaxation time, or saturation must be measured and corrected. Exchange and unresolved overlap must be handled in the integrated areas. Proton and lithium spectra also require a stated relative calibration before raw numbers can be compared across nuclei.

Words: 310 Articles: 1
52 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 310
d OurBigBook.com
The zero-ppm signals E are plausibly solvated lithium halide, predominantly LiBr or LiI and their solution ion-pair/aggregate forms. Structural symmetry predicts one Li environment in A, two in B in a 3:1 ratio, two in C in a 2:2 ratio, and one in an ideal symmetric D.
The natural lithium assignment is therefore:
  • Br mixture: A at approximately 1.68ppm (43.4); B at approximately 0.80 (16.2, three Li) and 1.55 (5.4, one Li); D at 0.73 (10.3, broad); E at 0.00 (24.8).
  • I mixture: A at approximately 1.68 (59.9); B at approximately 1.10 (8.4, three Li) and 1.55 (2.8, one Li); C at approximately 1.0 and 0.35 (0.6 each); D at 0.97 (2.3, broad); E at 0.00 (3.0). The close C/D signals require care about overlap.
The major proton peak near −2.08ppm is A. The next peak near −2.15 to −2.16 is naturally assigned to B; in the iodide mixture the smaller peaks near −2.22 and −2.28 distinguish C and D. Smaller D aggregates can exchange Li or ligands with free halide-containing species more rapidly, giving intermediate-exchange broadening at the two specifically identified broad lithium resonances.
There is a quantitative inconsistency in the printed integrations under these ideal single-species assignments. For example the Br lithium B integrals give molecular amount proportional to 5.4, while A gives 43.4/4=10.85. Their proton areas should consequently obey HB​/HA​=9(5.4)/[12(10.85)]=0.373, whereas either small proton integral gives 17/66=0.258. No common proton-versus-lithium calibration removes that ratio discrepancy. Similarly the I B/A ratio predicted from Li is 0.140, compared with printed 9/90=0.100.
Thus the symmetry-based assignment above is useful, but an exact simultaneous quantitative assignment satisfying every printed reliable integral is not established by these data. It would require corrected integrals, an explicitly overlapped signal or an additional speciation model; the discrepancy should not be concealed by treating independently normalized spectra as automatically consistent.

e

Words: 157 Articles: 1
52 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 157
e OurBigBook.com
In the slowly exchanging cubane A each methyl carbon is bonded to three equivalent 6Li nuclei with I=1. Its single carbon environment gives a septet, with first-order intensities 1:3:6:7:6:3:1.
In B the three methyl vertices remain equivalent by the ideal threefold symmetry, but each carbon sees two equivalent Li of one type and one Li of the other. The carbon resonance is therefore a quintet of triplets (15 first-order lines if both couplings are resolved and unequal): the equivalent pair gives 1:2:3:2:1, and the third Li gives 1:1:1. Accidental equality of couplings can collapse this to a septet.
D has one methyl-carbon environment coupled to two equivalent Li, giving a quintet 1:2:3:2:1. E has no methyl carbon. These patterns assume proton decoupling, resolved 1JCLi​, ideal aggregate symmetry and slow exchange; without proton decoupling each methyl-carbon pattern is additionally split by its three attached protons.

i

Words: 261 Articles: 1
a OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 261
i OurBigBook.com
The first transformation is an Achmatowicz rearrangement, followed by protection and selective reduction; the last is a Johnson-Claisen rearrangement.
  • Butyllithium removes the furan 2-proton, giving a 2-lithiofuran. Its carbon attacks the aldehyde carbonyl; protonation of the resulting alkoxide gives the furfuryl alcohol. Carbon-carbon bond formation occurs at the lithiated position.
  • Electrophilic oxygen transfer from mCPBA to the electron-rich furan gives an oxidized, ring-opened intermediate. Opening the oxygenated furan gives a hydroxy enedicarbonyl: the original furfuryl hydroxyl then attacks the remote aldehyde intramolecularly. This expands the five-membered furan into a six-membered lactol containing an enone carbonyl. The original furfuryl oxygen becomes the pyran ring oxygen; oxidation of the furan supplies the new carbonyl and lactol functionality.
  • Ag2​O/MeI converts the lactol OH into its methyl acetal: oxygen attacks methyl iodide by SN2 reaction, with iodide removal and proton transfer. This protects the anomeric position.
  • LiAlH4​ delivers hydride to the remaining ketone carbonyl, followed by protonation. The methyl acetal survives these basic reducing conditions, leaving the depicted allylic alcohol.
  • Under weak-acid catalysis, that allylic OH replaces an ethoxy group of triethyl orthoacetate. Loss of another ethanol molecule, with removal of a methyl proton, gives the mixed ketene acetal CH2​=C(OEt)−O−(allyl). A six-electron, chair-like Claisen rearrangement breaks the allyl-O bond, forms a bond between the terminal allyl carbon and the ketene-acetal CH2​, and moves the ring double bond one position. Carbonyl formation gives the −CH2​CO2​Et substituent.
The acetal protects the other oxygenated position during hydride reduction. The orthoester transfers an acetate-derived two-carbon unit through a ketene acetal; it does not directly substitute the allylic OH with an intact acetate ion.
[ref]

ii

Words: 159 Articles: 1
a OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 159
ii OurBigBook.com
For a concrete choice, draw the intermediate in the planar ring orientation used in the question and put the allylic OH on the upper face, with a solid-wedge C-OH bond. Fix either configuration at the R-bearing and methoxy-bearing centres and retain it throughout; no absolute configuration is specified by the question.
Draw the six-membered rearrangement array with its allylic C-C-C segment along the same ring edge and the O-ketene-acetal tether above that edge. Suprafacial transfer forms the new ring-carbon–CH2​CO2​Et bond on that upper face: draw it as a solid wedge, replacing the original allylic OH with the shifted double bond. The R-bearing and methoxy-bearing stereocentres retain their configurations. The opposite OH epimer transfers the tether from the opposite face and gives the opposite new stereocentre. Favor the chair-like transition structure that puts the larger tether substituents outward. This explicitly correlates the selected OH face with the new bond rather than invoking a freely rotating allylic carbocation.

iii

Words: 78 Articles: 1
a OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 78
iii OurBigBook.com
Propionic acid is a weak, relatively high-boiling acid: its normal boiling point is about 141∘C, compared with about 118∘C for acetic acid. It provides mild proton catalysis while remaining in the hot orthoester mixture more effectively. This is useful because ketene-acetal formation and the thermal Johnson-Claisen rearrangement require heating, whereas strong acid would threaten the pyran acetal.
This is a practical catalyst choice, not an absolute mechanistic prohibition on acetic acid; acetic-acid-catalysed orthoester rearrangements are also possible.

Solution
Words: 107
i OurBigBook.com
Write Im for an imidazolyl group. The acid protonates one imidazole nitrogen, and its carboxylate attacks the central carbonyl of carbonyldiimidazole. Collapse of the tetrahedral intermediate expels imidazole and gives the mixed anhydride RCO−O−CO−Im. Acyl transfer to imidazole, with decarboxylation, produces the activated acyl imidazole RCO−Im, CO2​ and imidazole.
The amine attacks the RCO carbonyl of that acyl imidazole. Its tetrahedral intermediate collapses with loss of imidazole; proton transfer gives RCONHR′. The carbonyl originally belonging to CDI leaves as CO2​, while the product amide carbonyl is the original acid carbonyl. Imidazole serves both as a leaving group and a proton-transfer base.

Occupied-to-occupied rotations only change the representation of the same occupied subspace; the occupied-virtual rotations describe distinct nearby determinants.

Stability in this space does not by itself prove global minimality or stability under more general spin/complex-orbital variations.

Suppose two potentials v,v′ differing by more than a constant have different ground states Ψ,Ψ′ but the same density ρ. Strict Rayleigh-Ritz variational principle inequalities give
E<E′+∫[v(r)−v′(r)]ρ(r)d3r,

E′<E+∫[v′(r)−v(r)]ρ(r)d3r.
(36)

In the usual exchange-hole representation, the hole around an electron integrates to charge deficit −1. Far outside a finite system, the localized hole therefore looks like a unit opposite charge at distance r. The Coulomb interaction has leading scale −1/r, and the exchange pair energy carries the usual factor 1/2 to avoid double counting, giving exchange energy per electron −1/(2r).
This energy-per-electron tail should not be confused with the exchange or exchange-correlation potential, whose leading coefficient is generally −1/r in the corresponding exact finite-system setting. Local energy-density representations also require a specified gauge; the question uses the conventional exchange-hole interpretation.

Close-packed layers occupy one of three lateral registries, conventionally A, B and C. Hexagonal close packing has ABAB stacking, while face-centered cubic stacking is ABCABC. On a bulk-terminated (111) terrace the two kinds of threefold hollow differ by subsurface registry: an hcp hollow places an atom above a second-layer atom, while an fcc hollow continues the ABC sequence.
Compressing the top Au layer makes its registry drift relative to the unreconstructed layers. Parts of the cell occupy fcc hollows, others hcp hollows, and transition strips pass through less favorable bridge-like positions. Those registry changes are associated with partial-dislocation/domain boundaries. Varying local coordination and repulsion from the substrate cause vertical relaxation, producing the observed corrugation rather than an entirely flat shifted sheet.

Periodically changing boundary direction among equivalent orientations redistributes that strain and lowers its long-range elastic cost, while boundary formation and bending carry their own energy cost.
The resulting compromise produces the characteristic herringbone arrangement. Threefold symmetry explains the equivalent turning directions; a balance of elastic relaxation and boundary costs, rather than symmetry alone, sets the finite repeat distance.

The cycle changes alkene geometry without requiring cleavage of either original labeled C-H bond. Since two positions are labeled, 0.86 is a combined effect; equal independent contributions would each be 0.86​=0.927.
The isotope effect supports an addition/elimination route rather than simple rotation of an intact double bond; it does not, alone, identify every proton-transfer order.

Solution

Words: 126
c OurBigBook.com
The natural mechanism is ionizing solvolysis: C-OTs cleavage gives a cyclopentyl cation/ion pair, capture by acetic acid gives the protonated acetate ester, and deprotonation gives product.
The 1.15 effect from H/D at the leaving-group carbon is normal alpha-secondary: that carbon develops trigonal carbocation character. The 2.06 effect from four neighboring labels is a combined beta-secondary effect. Adjacent C-H sigma bonds stabilize the developing empty p orbital by hyperconjugation; replacing H by D changes the vibrational stabilization and slows ionization. If the four contributions were equal and independent, each would be 2.061/4=1.198.
None of those labeled C-H bonds is broken. The isotope effects support substantial carbocation character, although distinguishing a free cation from an intimate ion pair needs additional evidence.

Solution

Words: 133
d OurBigBook.com
Bridgehead substitution proceeds by ionization and solvent capture; backside displacement at the adamantyl bridgehead is geometrically inaccessible. The rigid cage prevents the labeled bonds from sampling all the favorable alignments available in cyclopentyl solvolysis.
The two labeled bonds in the adjacent methylene group are poorly oriented for ordinary C-H-to-empty-orbital hyperconjugation, explaining an effect close to 1.000. Cage C-C sigma donation and geometrical relaxation can still stabilize the developing adamantyl cation. The three remote bridgehead labels perturb that coupled framework and give the smaller normal effect 1.073, or about 1.024 per label if contributions are equivalent.
This is a geometrical and remote secondary isotope effect. It does not imply cleavage of the remote C-H bonds, and absence of a beta effect at one selected site does not establish absence of a cation.

Words: 153
e OurBigBook.com
Triethylamine attacks the benzyl carbon and bromide leaves, giving the quaternary benzyltriethylammonium salt. A useful substitution transition structure is
[Et3​N⋯C(L)2​(Ar)⋯Br]‡,
(64)
with developing N-C bonding and breaking C-Br bonding. The C-H/D bonds remain intact, so the small effects are secondary.
For X=NO2​, a relatively associative SN2 reaction transition state can give a small inverse effect, 0.988, through altered bending constraints. The unsubstituted case, 0.993, is close to cancellation of opposing contributions. Electron-donating OMe stabilizes benzylic positive charge, favoring a looser, more dissociative transition state and a slightly normal effect, 1.014; it also explains the increased relative rate, 7.4 versus 1 for H and 0.52 for NO2​.
Thus the data indicate increasing dissociative character with electron donation. A contribution from a separate ionization pathway is possible for the strongest donor, but these small isotope effects and three relative rates do not uniquely require a sharp SN2-to-SN1 mechanism switch.
